rules.title: How to play
rules.heading: Abalone rules: how to play
rules.intro: Abalone is a two-player strategy game on a hexagonal board. Each player has 14 marbles. You win by pushing six of your opponent's marbles off the board. This page explains every rule. When you are ready, <online>play Abalone online</online> or <offline>try it against the computer</offline>.

goal.title: The goal
goal.body: Push six of your opponent's marbles off the edge of the board. The first player to do it wins. You cannot win by trapping marbles, only by pushing them out.

turns.title: Who moves first
turns.body: Players take turns, one move each. Black goes first. On your turn you must move; you cannot pass.

directions.title: How marbles move
directions.body: A marble moves one space to any of the six neighbouring spaces. The board is a hexagon, so each space touches six others. There are no jumps and no captures by jumping.
directions.caption: The six directions.

move.title: Moving one, two or three marbles
move.body: You may move one, two or three of your own marbles in one turn. Two or three marbles must touch in a straight line, and they move together one space. There are two kinds of move:
move.inline: In-line move: the group moves along the line it points, like a train. The front marble steps into the next space.
move.broadside: Side step (broadside): the group moves sideways, each marble into the empty space next to it. All the target spaces must be empty.
move.limit: You can never move more than three marbles, and never marbles that are not in a straight line.
move.inline_caption: In line: the row advances the way it points.
move.broadside_caption: Broadside: the row steps sideways onto empty spaces.

push.title: Pushing: the sumito
push.body: A push is called a sumito. It is an in-line move into a space held by your opponent. You need more marbles in the line than your opponent:
push.conditions: Two more conditions: the space behind the pushed marbles must be empty (or off the board), and the push must be in line, never a side step. Equal numbers never push, so 2 against 2 and 3 against 3 are a standoff. You can never push your own marbles.
push.ok_caption: Three against two: the line shifts one space.
push.blocked_caption: Equal numbers never move, and you never push your own.

capture.title: Pushing marbles off the board
capture.body: If a push moves an opposing marble past the edge, it is out of the game. That is one point toward your six. A marble next to the edge is in danger: if you are pushed there with fewer marbles than your opponent has in line, you lose it.
capture.caption: Two against one at the edge: black is out.

win.title: How to win
win.body: The first player to push six marbles off wins. If you cannot stop a push, break the line: move a marble next to the attacker so it is outnumbered, or pull back from the edge.

setups.title: Starting positions
setups.body: Every layout starts with 14 marbles each.
setups.standard: <name>Standard:</name> each side starts on its two nearest rows (black at the bottom, white at the top), with three marbles in the middle of the third row. The armies face each other and no pushing is possible on move one. Best for learning.
setups.belgian_daisy: <name>Belgian daisy:</name> marbles start in four flower-shaped clusters, one in each corner. Black and white alternate around the board (white top-left and bottom-right, black top-right and bottom-left). The armies touch on the first move, so play is fast and tactical. Popular in tournaments because it is fairer than the standard layout.
setups.german_daisy: <name>German daisy:</name> four flower-shaped clusters again, with the same colours as the Belgian daisy (white upper left and lower right, black upper right and lower left), but set in from the corners toward the sides. The clusters start further apart, so the opening is more open.
setups.others: Others in the game: Dutch daisy, Swiss daisy, Alien, Domination, Infiltration and The Wall. Choose one when you start a game.

diagonal.question: Can I move marbles diagonally?
diagonal.answer: Every direction on the hexagon grid counts as one of six directions; there is no other kind of diagonal.

single.question: Can a single marble push?
single.answer: No. A push needs at least two marbles against one.

own_block.question: What if my push is blocked by my own marble?
own_block.answer: Then it is not a legal move.

solved.question: Is Abalone solved?
solved.answer: No. It is a deep game with plenty to learn. Try the strategy tips: <strategy>Abalone strategy: 7 tips</strategy>.

strategy.title: Strategy
strategy.heading: Abalone strategy: 7 tips to win
strategy.intro: Abalone looks simple and is not. These seven habits take most beginners from losing marbles to winning pushes. Practise each one in a <offline>free game against the computer</offline>. New to the game? Read the <rules>Abalone rules</rules> first.

center.title: 1. Control the center
center.body: Marbles in the middle have six neighbours and room to move. Marbles on the edge are one push from out. Early on, move your outer marbles toward the center and keep the opponent's off it. A player who owns the center decides where the fight happens.

groups_of_three.title: 2. Keep your groups of three
groups_of_three.body: Three connected marbles in a line can push two, and cannot easily be pushed. Move so your marbles stay in compact, touching groups. A lone marble is a target, and a long thin chain is easy to cut.

edge.title: 3. Stay away from the edge
edge.body: Every marble on the outer ring can be lost to a single sumito. Only go there to attack, and only when your push comes first. If your marble is on the edge and your opponent has a line pointing at it, move it or block the line this turn.

count.title: 4. Count before you push
count.body: A push needs more marbles in line than your opponent, and an empty space behind. Before each push, count both lines and check what your move leaves open. A push that breaks up your own group often gives the marble straight back.

opening.title: 5. Choose your opening on purpose
opening.body: In the standard layout, nobody can push on move one, so develop toward the center in small steps and keep your three-marble rows. In a Belgian daisy the armies touch at once: look for the first sumito and defend your weakest cluster. Try each layout against the computer to learn what changes.

attack_as_a_group.title: 6. Attack as a group, not as a hero
attack_as_a_group.body: Pushing one marble off with a lone stack of three is rare. More often you win by pressuring an edge marble with two groups, so your opponent cannot answer both. Bring a second line to the same area before you commit.

tempo.title: 7. Win the tempo, not the marble
tempo.body: Do not rush for the first point. A player who leads by a marble but has scattered groups often loses the next three exchanges. Make safe moves that leave your opponent with only bad ones; Abalone is a game of who runs out of good moves first.

items.lone_edge: Moving a marble alone to the edge to "threaten" something.
items.split_three: Splitting a three into two twos just before the opponent's three arrives.
items.leave_hole: Pushing when it leaves a hole your opponent steps into.

guide.title: How to move
guide.select_body: Tap one of your marbles. Tap up to two more in a straight line to move them together.
guide.direction_body: Tap a highlighted space to move there. A longer line can push a shorter line of your opponent's.
guide.win_body: Push six of your opponent's marbles off the edge of the board and you win.
